perfinr

Source: vignettes/perfinr.qmd

perfinr holds the R functions from Personal Finance: a field manual. Each chapter of the book builds its calculations from scratch so you can see how the formula works. This package collects those same functions, documents them, and tests them, so you can use them without copying code out of the book. In this vignette I’ll cover how to install perfinr and the conventions every function follows. Then we’ll take a short tour with one example from each part of the book.

Installation

perfinr isn’t on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("mjfrigaard/perfinr")

perfinr has no dependencies beyond base R.

Conventions

The functions keep the names, arguments, and defaults from the book, so code from a chapter runs unchanged after library(perfinr). A few rules hold across the whole package:

Rule Example
Rates and returns are decimals 0.07 is 7%
The one exception is rule_of_72(), which takes a percent rule_of_72(7)
Ratio functions return percents percent_of_income(1500, 5000) returns 30, not 0.30
Most functions are vectorized future_value(10000, 0.07, c(10, 20)) returns two values
A few functions take single values only income_tax(), raise_kept(), payoff_vs_invest(), first_payment_split()
A 0% rate returns the no interest answer mortgage_payment(120000, 0, 30) is 120000 / 360
Bad inputs stop with an error text, NA, or a zero where a divisor is needed

Vectorized functions make it easy to compare options side by side. Here is the same $10,000 at 7% over four horizons:

data.frame(
  years = c(5, 10, 20, 30),
  value = future_value(present_value = 10000, rate = 0.07, years = c(5, 10, 20, 30))
)
#>   years    value
#> 1     5 14025.52
#> 2    10 19671.51
#> 3    20 38696.84
#> 4    30 76122.55

When an input doesn’t make sense, the function says which argument is wrong instead of returning Inf or NaN:

percent_of_income(expense = 1500, income = 0)
#> Error:
#> ! `income` must be greater than 0.

How the vignettes map to the book

There is one vignette for each chapter of the book. Each one takes the chapter’s examples (with the same numbers), shows the bar model, and then answers the question with perfinr functions.

A short tour

Each example below uses the numbers from the book, so you can check the result against the chapter.

Foundations

Rent of $1,500 on a $5,000 monthly income:

rent_share <- percent_of_income(expense = 1500, income = 5000)
rent_share
#> [1] 30

Rent takes 30% of income. A $5,000 credit card balance at 22% APR, paying $100 a month:

payoff <- months_to_payoff(balance = 5000, monthly_payment = 100, apr = 0.22)
payoff
#> [1] 136.7791

That is about 11.4 years of payments.

Savings

Spending $2,720 of a $3,200 take home paycheck:

savings_rate(income = 3200, spending = 2720)
#> [1] 15

Investing

$10,000 invested at 7% for 10 years:

future_value(present_value = 10000, rate = 0.07, years = 10)
#> [1] 19671.51

Taxes and insurance

2026 federal income tax on a $45,000 salary (single filer), and the effective rate:

tax <- income_tax(income = 45000)
tax
#> [1] 3220
tax / 45000
#> [1] 0.07155556

The effective rate is 7.2%, well below the 12% top bracket this salary reaches.

Planning

The monthly payment on a $480,000 mortgage at 6% over 30 years:

mortgage_payment(principal = 480000, annual_rate = 0.06, years = 30)
#> [1] 2877.843

Recap

perfinr gives you the book’s functions as a tested package. Rates go in as decimals, ratios come out as percents, and most functions accept vectors so you can compare options in one call. The chapter vignettes walk through each part of the book in the same order as the chapters.
